intro: The finale takes over the slow movement’s unresolved chord and turns it into continuous semiquaver motion. Beethoven repeats the development and recapitulation, not the exposition, before a faster Presto coda.
question: How does continuous motion accommodate a development, a return and a written repeat?

sections.label: Introduction · inherited dissonance
sections.mNote: The slow movement’s diminished seventh launches running figures

sections.label: Exposition
sections.mNote: F-minor first group and C-minor second group share semiquaver motion

sections.label: Development · first traversal
sections.mNote: Fragments and a chordal idea lead to dominant preparation

sections.label: Recapitulation · first traversal
sections.mNote: Both thematic groups return to the F-minor home region

sections.label: Development · repeated
sections.mNote: The written repeat restarts the development, not the exposition

sections.label: Recapitulation · repeated
sections.mNote: The recapitulation is traversed again before a different ending

sections.label: Coda · Presto
sections.mNote: A new compact idea precedes the final F-minor drive

cues.title: Dissonance carried across
cues.text: The finale begins with the diminished-seventh harmony left unresolved by the Andante. Repeated chords release a running line, which prepares the F-minor main subject. The movement grows out of the previous ending rather than starting from a settled tonic.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 16–17, shows attacca and the shared diminished chord: https://www.beethoven.de/en/media/view/6661552451092480?page=0 . The report’s opening is active and forceful, then falls around 0:15 before the main span. Separate MP3 boundaries do not establish a gapless digital join.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A line that keeps running
cues.text: Through the first group, semiquavers carry the motion while the hands exchange their roles. Listen for changes in register and accent inside the stream. The persistent note-value does not mean that every phrase has the same direction or weight.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 17–18, passes the running material between the hands. The report shows a comparatively continuous level across 0:20–0:45, after the introductory dip; this cue concerns that span, not an individual hand change.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A second group without repose
cues.text: The second group moves to C minor, the minor dominant of F, but retains the semiquaver motion. A change of key and melodic shape therefore does not bring the kind of slower lyrical contrast heard in the first movement.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 18–19, gives the C-minor second group over continuing semiquavers. The report’s 0:50 boundary precedes this later exposition span, with stronger level around 1:05–1:20; the harmony comes from the score, not the key estimator.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The sonata in print
cues.text: The original edition appeared in Vienna in 1807, published by the Bureau des Arts et d’Industrie. Its plate number is 521. The score’s repeat signs and final Presto belong to that early printed text, not to a modern editor’s reconstruction.
cues.evidence: IMSLP General Information dates the first publication to 1807: https://imslp.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No.23%2C_Op.57_%28Beethoven%2C_Ludwig_van%29 . Beethoven-Haus identifies and displays the original edition, plate 521: https://www.beethoven.de/en/media/view/6661552451092480?page=0 .

cues.title: Motion at the quietest level
cues.text: Near the development’s end, Beethoven reduces the texture and prolongs dominant harmony. The running impulse survives at a much lower level before the main material returns. Listen through the thinning passage rather than treating its withdrawal as an ending.
cues.evidence: First edition, p. 21, supplies the quiet dominant preparation. The 2:18 novelty peak begins a substantial withdrawal, with low-level windows at 2:35–2:40 before the 2:46 return boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Home key, continuing motion
cues.text: The recapitulation brings back the main F-minor material without stopping the semiquavers. Its later second group will also be placed in F minor. The tonal route changes, but the movement’s running texture remains the connecting thread.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 21–24, restores the first group and subsequently transposes the second group into F minor. The report’s 2:46 novelty peak and sharp level rise around 2:45–2:50 anchor the approximate return.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cycles before these records
cues.text: Schnabel played all thirty-two Beethoven piano sonatas in Berlin in 1927 and returned to a complete cycle there in 1933. His HMV recordings grew alongside a concert repertory organised around the whole sequence, not this sonata alone.
cues.evidence: The Schnabel Music Foundation biography documents the Berlin cycles of 1927 and January–April 1933: https://schnabelmusicfoundation.org/musicians/artur-schnabel/ . The selected Archive item identifies the HMV Beethoven Sonata Society recording cycle: https://archive.org/details/beethovenschnabel6 .

cues.title: Back to the development
cues.text: The written repeat takes the music back to the development, not to the beginning of the movement. The changing-key material and the return must now be traversed again. Beethoven gives the unstable middle and its resolution the repetition usually reserved for an exposition.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 20 and 24, places the start-repeat at the development and the first ending after the recapitulation. The report’s 3:52 boundary and subsequent contour correspond to 1:24 onward; the quiet preparations at 2:18–2:40 and 4:44–5:10 also recur. The repeat order is score-supported and timing remains approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The preparation heard again
cues.text: On this traversal, the development again contracts towards its quiet dominant preparation. Recognise the process as well as the notes: growing pressure, thinning texture and a held harmonic direction lead towards the F-minor return a second time.
cues.evidence: The repeated first-edition development reaches the same retransition on p. 21. The report has its highest level around 4:30–4:35, then a sharp drop at the 4:44 boundary and a sustained quiet stretch to 5:10, paralleling the earlier preparation.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The return heard again
cues.text: The recapitulation reappears after the repeated development. Its thematic order remains familiar, but this traversal eventually takes a different ending: instead of sending the music back once more, Beethoven directs it towards an acceleration and the Presto coda.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 21–24, supplies the repeated recapitulation and alternative endings. The report’s 5:12 and 5:16 novelty peaks and level rise around 5:15 support the second return; the alternative ending occurs later, not at this cue time.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The sonata on radio
cues.text: A New Zealand programme listing for 30 December 1934 advertises “An Hour with Beethoven”, featuring Schnabel playing the “Appassionata”. The notice names performer and work but gives no record catalogue number.
cues.evidence: Radio Record, 28 December 1934, p. 22, Sunday 30 December, alternative programme 1YX at 8 p.m.: https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/periodicals/RADREC19341228.2.42 . This corroborates contemporary public presence, not the identity of the transferred pressing or a first-release day.

cues.title: A different closing idea
cues.text: The coda’s Presto introduces a compact chordal idea, with short repeated phrases, before the running semiquavers regain the foreground. The change of texture makes the faster tempo more than a simple continuation of the preceding passage.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 24–25, gives sempre più allegro, Presto and the new repeated idea. The report falls from its 6:15–6:20 crest into a lower-level span at 6:25–6:40, with a boundary at 6:32; 6:24 is a provisional score-proportion estimate of the Presto onset.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: No turn to major
cues.text: The last drive ends with forceful F-minor chords, not a change to F major. Listen to the low-register descent and the final separation of attacks. The sonata closes in the same minor key in which its first quiet phrase began.
cues.evidence: First edition, p. 25, shows the final descent and F-minor closing chords. The report marks a change at 6:44, continuing activity through 6:55 and final decay around 7:00; the noise floor is reached by 7:05 within the 430.9-second file.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Diminished harmony releases the running subject
transitions.how: The diminished seventh inherited from the Andante releases running figures that lead towards the dominant of F minor. After the introductory surge, Beethoven reduces the dynamic level and begins the main subject without abandoning the semiquavers. Harmonic resolution and a quieter texture distinguish the subject from its preparation; the continuous small notes carry the join.
transitions.evidence: First edition, p. 17, supplies the introduction and quiet F-minor main subject: https://www.beethoven.de/en/media/view/6661552451092480?page=0 . The report’s drop around 0:15 and more continuous level from 0:20 anchor an approximate 0:16 boundary.

transitions.title: The closing stream changes harmonic direction
transitions.how: The exposition’s C-minor closing material runs into a linking passage instead of an exposition repeat. The continuing figures redirect the harmony towards B♭ minor, where the development begins. Beethoven subsequently adds a more chordal idea, but the bass and semiquaver motion keep the change of section connected to what came before. The repeat sign here marks the start of the later repeated span.
transitions.evidence: First edition, pp. 19–20, supplies the link, start-repeat and development. The report’s strongest novelty peak at 1:24 separates the preceding high-level close from a lower-level restart around 1:25–1:35. The B♭-minor reading comes from the score.

transitions.title: Quiet dominant preparation yields to F minor
transitions.how: The development’s figures thin out over dominant preparation on C. Beethoven reduces the dynamic level almost to disappearance before restoring the main F-minor subject. The semiquaver motion provides continuity, but the return of the theme and tonic gives that motion a renewed direction. The later second group is rewritten in the home minor rather than the exposition’s C minor.
transitions.evidence: First edition, p. 21, supplies the quiet preparation and returning subject. Relative level reaches approximately −37 dB at 2:35–2:40, then rises to −16.4 at 2:45 and −11.1 at 2:50; the report marks a strong boundary at 2:46.

transitions.title: The first ending turns back
transitions.how: The first ending after the recapitulation replaces a final close with a diminishing, descending link. The repeat sends that line back to the development’s opening, recovering its B♭-minor region rather than restarting the F-minor exposition. Beethoven repeats the entire development-and-return span, so the harmonic instability must be worked through again before the music can reach its coda.
transitions.evidence: First edition, p. 24, first ending, returns to the start-repeat on p. 20. The 3:52 novelty peak and level drop correspond to the 1:24 development boundary, followed by a closely matching broad contour. The written repeat and measured recurrence jointly support the order.

transitions.title: The dominant prepares the same return
transitions.how: The repeated development again reaches the quiet C-dominant preparation and restores the F-minor main subject. This is the same written return, not a new development or an additional theme. The difference lies ahead: at the recapitulation’s end, the second ending will continue forwards instead of taking the descending route back to the development.
transitions.evidence: First edition, p. 21, is traversed again before the second ending on p. 24. The report’s quiet stretch at 4:45–5:10 is followed by novelty peaks at 5:12 and 5:16 and a large level rise at 5:15. The boundary is approximate.

transitions.title: The second ending accelerates instead
transitions.how: The second ending retains the running figures but asks for sempre più allegro, carrying the recapitulation forwards rather than back to the repeat. Presto then brings a new chordal idea in F minor, organised in short repeated phrases. The change of texture briefly makes the faster pulse easier to grasp before the semiquaver stream returns for the final drive.
transitions.evidence: First edition, p. 24, supplies the second ending, sempre più allegro, Presto and its repeated phrases. The report’s 6:15–6:20 crest gives way to lower level and changing onset activity around 6:25–6:40, including a 6:32 novelty peak. The 6:24 join is a provisional passage estimate, not a bar-aligned claim.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The selected file’s artist tag, Archive description and Bloesch agree. The session list records a Bechstein piano, without an established serial number.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The original solo-piano finale is identified, but the performing edition and editorial alterations are not documented. Commentary uses the original edition, plate 521. Its repeat of development plus recapitulation is supported by recurring contours in this recording’s analysis; this does not identify Schnabel’s score or establish an edit/take-splice history. The source’s attacca from movement II is distinct from separate-file playback spacing.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Archive’s specific Op. 57 description gives 11.IV.1933, corroborated by the discography and reissue documentation. The general compilation date 1932 is not used for this sonata. The embedded date tag 2001 and repository upload in 2020 do not establish a session or transfer date.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Abbey Road Studios, Studio No. 3, London, England
fields.note: Bloesch’s work entry identifies Abbey Road Studios, London, and the chronological session list specifies Studio No. 3 and a Bechstein piano.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: His Master’s Voice issued the original recording. The actual pressing or subsequent reissue used to produce the selected MP3 is not identified, so its source-carrier label remains unknown.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The historical complete-sonata issue was HMV DB 2215–2217 in Beethoven Sonata Society Volume 5, part of set DB 2211–2217. That original catalogue is documented, but no source-carrier or reissue catalogue is established for this digital file.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: Bloesch assigns the finale to historical sides 2B 6609 and 2B 6610, takes 1; the release-set catalogue lists 2B 6609I and 2B 6610I. Those original issued-side identifiers do not independently establish the take identities, source pressing or side-join location in this MP3.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified for the selected file. Archive uploader recordplayer78 is not assumed to be its engineer or owner. The independently consulted Pristine transfer credits Andrew Rose, but no upstream relationship with this MP3 is documented; that credit is not imported.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item was added/public on 27 March 2020. Its MP3 carries date tag 2001 without identifying the event or release represented. Neither date is accepted as the analogue-transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: The embedded encoder tag states ‘Audiograbber 1.83.01, LAME dll 3.99, 256 Kbit/s, Joint Stereo, Normal quality’.
fields.note: The inspected selected stream contains MP3 audio at 44,100 Hz, two channels and 256,000 bit/s, with an attached JPEG image. Joint-stereo encoding is not evidence of an original stereo session. Analogue equipment, equalisation, restoration, noise reduction, speed/pitch correction and edit history remain unknown. Archive’s inventory calls the file ‘VBR MP3’; that repository label is distinguished from the stream and embedded encoder information.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: The underlying Beethoven composition is public domain under the ordinary EU life-plus-70 term.
fields.note: Beethoven died in 1827. The viewable original score supplies historical musical evidence, not clearance of an unidentified modern performing edition. The composition’s term is separate from the recording’s rights.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: original sound recording first published in 1934.
fields.note: The Public Domain Project release-set catalogue explicitly states first release in 1934 for HMV DB 2211–2217. Bloesch identifies Op. 57 as DB 2215–2217, matrices 2B 6605–6610, distinguishing publication evidence from the 11 April 1933 session. Under the programme’s territorial EU rule, the earlier 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension. US status is not established and no worldwide clearance is claimed. The Archive Public Domain Mark is not an ownership release; the Public Domain Project’s worldwide/US expiry table is not adopted. No CC licence or independently established additional rights in an unidentified modern transfer are asserted.

facts: Christian Gottlob Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792 · Vienna and its surrounding villages thereafter
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · one opera
Progressive hearing loss documented in letters from 1801; conversation books used from 1818
composer.background:
Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770, probably on 16 December, and baptised on 17 December. His father Johann sang in the electoral court chapel, and his grandfather Ludwig had been its Kapellmeister. The family name came from the Low Countries; the ‘van’ did not indicate nobility. Johann attempted to present his son as a child prodigy, but Beethoven’s more substantial training came from Christian Gottlob Neefe, who introduced him to Bach’s keyboard music and helped him obtain work as an organist. Playing viola in the court orchestra also gave him practical knowledge of instrumental and operatic repertory.

The Bonn years supplied more than a musical apprenticeship. The court of Elector Maximilian Franz, educated patrons and friends such as the Breuning family brought Beethoven into contact with Enlightenment literature and social ideas. After his mother’s death in 1787 and his father’s worsening incapacity, he assumed increasing responsibility for the household. In 1792 he left for Vienna to study with Haydn. The intended period of further training became permanent residence: the French occupation of Bonn in 1794 ended the old electoral establishment to which he might have returned.
composer.epithet: A pianist who turned small rhythmic cells into long arguments, then rebuilt the forms that contained them.
